type_rationale: The main contribution is a minimal anisotropic phase-field model coupled to latent-heat diffusion, supported by a sharp-interface interpretation and applied to two-dimensional dendritic solidification morphology.
must_cover: Diffuse solid-liquid interface and double-well free energy
Phase-field and heat equations with latent-heat coupling
Explicit/implicit numerical scheme and mesh limits
Effects of latent heat, anisotropy, and noise on dendrite morphology
Transfer boundary from pure-melt solidification to electrochemical phase separation
key_numbers: dimensionless latent heat K sampled around 0.8 to 2.0
central_claims: A two-field diffuse-interface model can generate varied dendritic morphologies without explicit interface tracking.
Small changes in anisotropy strongly reorganize branch direction and competition.
Noise controls side-branch selection in non-oscillating growth but is less influential when tip oscillation supplies a stronger branching mechanism.
claim_boundaries: The calculations are qualitative rather than quantitatively converged.
The model excludes flow, mechanics, composition, electrochemical potential, and reaction kinetics.
Snowflake-like shapes are not a model of vapor-grown snowflakes.
mechanism_result_map: Double well plus gradient energy -> finite diffuse interface -> topology changes without front tracking.
Temperature-dependent driving plus latent-heat diffusion -> moving thermal field -> growth instability controlled by K.
Angular epsilon and capillary derivatives -> oriented surface tension -> dendrite selection and corners.
Interface-localized noise -> unequal branch competition -> side-branch selection.
comparative_positioning: Avoids explicit moving-boundary bookkeeping when fronts merge or split.
Provides a diffuse-interface approximation linked to a sharp-interface curvature law.
Prioritizes minimal morphology-generating physics over detailed material-specific fidelity.
negative_or_limiting_results: Features comparable to interface thickness are artificially smoothed or buried.
Reported discretization does not precisely approximate interface velocity.
Only a small subset of parameter space is explored and no direct experimental calibration is performed.
visual_plan: Page 2 for phase-field interface and double-well potential
Figure 7 on page 8 for anisotropy-driven morphology transition
Figures 10-11 on page 12 for noise sensitivity and capillary anisotropy
Page 13 for the author's numerical-resolution limitations
section_plan: Free energy, coupled equations, and sharp-interface interpretation
Morphology results, validation level, and mechanisms
Transfer value to battery phase-field research and resources
